beats.title: Stake build
beats.situation: Meridian Dynamics trades at 42 — half of sum-of-parts. Your fund holds 6.5%. Time to size the position before anyone notices the accumulation.
beats.debateTopic: How fast and how loud do we build the stake?

scriptedLines.text: Volume is thin. We can add 2% without moving the tape if we drip it over two weeks.
Or we file the 13D now and let the pop pay for the position.

options.label: Quietly accumulate to 8.5%
pros: Cheap entry before the market catches on
Board stays asleep a little longer
cons: Ties up a big slug of the war chest
Slow — no immediate catalyst
options.consequence: Unusual volume in MRDN goes unremarked; your stake quietly crosses 8%.

options.label: Build exposure via swaps and options
pros: Far cheaper on cash
Keeps footprint nearly invisible
cons: Less hard voting power when it matters
Disclosure fight if the GC smells derivatives
options.consequence: Prime brokers whisper about a mystery buyer in Meridian derivatives.

options.label: File the 13D now and announce 9%
pros: Instant credibility and a stock pop
Forces the board to engage on your clock
cons: Board goes straight into bunker mode
You pay top-of-tape prices to finish the stake
options.consequence: MRDN jumps 6% as your 13D hits the wire: 'intends to engage with management.'

beats.title: Private letter
beats.situation: CEO Marcus Hale agreed to a meeting. He thinks you are a tourist. The tone of your first letter will set the temperature of the whole campaign.
beats.debateTopic: Constructive engagement or a shot across the bow?

scriptedLines.text: We always welcome shareholder input. Through the proper channels, of course.
Translation: he'll bury us in IR boilerplate unless the letter has teeth.

options.label: Send a constructive private letter
pros: Keeps a settlement path open
Signals sophistication to the board
cons: Easy for Hale to slow-walk
No public pressure backing it
options.consequence: Hale acknowledges your letter and promises a 'thorough review of the ideas.'

options.label: Send a blunt demand letter
pros: No ambiguity about your intentions
Rattles the C-suite into mistakes
cons: Board circles the wagons early
Leaks make you look hostile
options.consequence: Your demand letter leaks within hours; Meridian calls it 'short-term financial engineering.'

options.label: Back-channel through the independent Chair
pros: Builds an ally inside the boardroom
Keeps Hale guessing
cons: Slow and deniable
Chair may report everything back to Hale
options.consequence: Chair Diane Okafor takes your call and listens longer than expected.

beats.title: Public thesis
beats.situation: The private track is moving slowly. Your 80-page thesis — margins, capital misallocation, the failing Orbital division — is ready. Publishing changes the campaign forever.
beats.debateTopic: Go public with the full thesis, leak selectively, or hold fire?

scriptedLines.text: The deck is airtight. Page 44 alone — Orbital's ROIC — ends the debate.
Once it's public there is no settling quietly. Everyone will be watching the tape.

options.label: Publish the full 80-page thesis
pros: Sets the narrative for the entire street
Other holders start doing your work for you
cons: Board hardens — no more quiet deals
You own every number in that deck now
options.consequence: MERIDIAN'S LOST DECADE hits every terminal; sell-side scrambles to update models.

options.label: Leak selective pages to a friendly columnist
pros: Pressure without full commitment
Deniability if numbers get challenged
cons: Half the impact of the full deck
Journalists hate being used and remember it
options.consequence: A well-sourced column asks why Meridian's Orbital division still exists.

options.label: Hold fire — keep working the private track
pros: Preserves goodwill from the letter
Board owes you one for the restraint
cons: Zero public pressure
Street starts wondering if you've gone soft
options.consequence: Silence from your fund; Meridian's IR team exhales — for now.

beats.title: Board seats vs review
beats.situation: Chair Okafor convenes a governance session. The board will entertain 'reasonable requests.' This is the moment to convert pressure into structural power.
beats.debateTopic: Demand board seats, a strategic review, or both?

scriptedLines.text: The board is prepared to discuss governance enhancements. Within reason.
Any demand letter will be evaluated against our fiduciary obligations — all of them.
Seats give us permanent leverage. A review gives us a catalyst. Pick your weapon.

options.label: Demand two board seats
pros: Permanent inside leverage
Signals long-term commitment to other holders
cons: Board fights nominee fights hardest
Insiders get slow-rolled by committee
options.consequence: You put forward two nominees; Meridian says the board is 'already well-composed.'

options.label: Demand a formal strategic review
pros: Creates a concrete catalyst with a deadline
Harder for the board to refuse publicly
cons: Reviews can be slow-walked into oblivion
No guarantee the conclusion favors you
options.consequence: Meridian announces a strategic review 'with independent advisors' — your fingerprints everywhere.

options.label: Demand both seats and a review
pros: Maximum pressure on every front
Whichever concession lands, you win
cons: Board unites against overreach
Expensive two-front campaign
options.consequence: Meridian's board calls your demands 'a hostile attempt to seize control without paying a premium.'

beats.title: Capital return vs breakup
beats.situation: CFO Priya Ramanathan controls the model. She privately concedes the balance sheet is lazy. What is the value-creation ask: return the cash, or break the company apart?
beats.debateTopic: Buyback and dividend, full breakup, or operational fix?

scriptedLines.text: We have 3.2 billion in cash earning nothing. I won't pretend otherwise.
Sum-of-parts says the pieces are worth 70. The conglomerate discount is the whole thesis.

options.label: Push a $2B buyback plus special dividend
pros: Immediate, mechanical support for the stock
CFO privately agrees — easy win
cons: One-time sugar hit, not a re-rating
Leaves the broken structure intact
options.consequence: Meridian 'evaluates capital return options'; the stock firms on the headline.

options.label: Push a breakup — spin off Orbital
pros: Unlocks the full sum-of-parts value
The review gives it procedural cover
cons: Multi-year execution risk
CEO will fight to keep his empire whole
options.consequence: Breakup speculation sends MRDN to a 52-week high; Hale calls the idea 'value-destructive.'

options.label: Push operational cost cuts
pros: Least confrontational value lever
Margin math is undeniable
cons: Slowest path to 60
Management claims credit for your plan
options.consequence: Meridian unveils a cost program suspiciously similar to page 61 of your deck.

beats.title: Curveball
beats.situation: Your analyst bursts into the war room. Something just hit the tape — and it changes the board math.
beats.debateTopic: React to the shock without losing the campaign.

scriptedLines.text: You need to see this. Right now.
Whatever it is — we decide fast and we decide once.

variants.title: Earnings shock
variants.situation: Meridian pre-announces a brutal Q3 miss — Orbital bleeding worse than even your model assumed. The stock gaps down.

options.label: Buy the dip aggressively
pros: Average down at panic prices
Bigger stake means bigger vote
cons: Burns serious war chest
Catching a falling knife if it worsens
options.consequence: Filings later reveal your fund bought the entire panic — stake now over 11%.

options.label: Press the mismanagement narrative
pros: The miss proves your thesis for free
Momentum with wavering holders
cons: Kicking them while down alienates the board
You look gleeful about bad news
options.consequence: 'WE TOLD YOU SO' — your statement runs everywhere next to Hale's grim guidance call.

variants.title: Poison pill adopted
variants.situation: Meridian's board adopts a 12% shareholder rights plan overnight — a poison pill aimed squarely at your fund.

options.label: Challenge the pill in Delaware
pros: Pills this naked rarely survive review
Discovery unearths board emails
cons: Litigation is slow and expensive
Judges dislike activists who sue first
options.consequence: Your Delaware complaint calls the pill 'an entrenchment device masquerading as governance.'

options.label: Negotiate a standstill for pill removal
pros: Defuses the crisis cheaply
Board reads it as good faith
cons: Caps your stake during the fight
Looks like blinking to the street
options.consequence: Meridian rescinds the pill; both sides announce 'constructive dialogue.'

variants.title: White-knight rumor
variants.situation: A wire report: Meridian has quietly courted a friendly acquirer at a modest premium — a white knight to dilute you out of the story.

options.label: Publicly oppose a sweetheart sale
pros: Blocks a lowball exit below intrinsic value
Rallies long-term holders to you
cons: You're now fighting a takeover premium
Arbs flood in with short horizons
options.consequence: Your open letter: 'Meridian is worth 70 broken up — not 52 in a fire sale to friends.'

options.label: Demand a formal auction process
pros: If it sells, it sells at the top
Puts the board's fiduciary duty on record
cons: Auction may attract a buyer you can't beat
Campaign becomes an M&A trade
options.consequence: You demand a full auction with independent bankers; the stock rips on deal math.

beats.title: Settle vs proxy
beats.situation: The nomination window opens in ten days. Chair Okafor floats a settlement framework. Take the deal on the table, or take it to a vote.
beats.debateTopic: Settle now or launch the proxy fight?

scriptedLines.text: There is a framework the board could live with. It requires both sides to stop performing.
If you go to a vote, we will run the full playbook. All of it.
Settlements are certain and small. Proxy fights are expensive and total.

options.label: Negotiate a settlement
pros: Locks in real gains without vote risk
Preserves capital for the next campaign
cons: Board keeps effective control
Street may read it as declaring victory early
options.consequence: Settlement announced: one board seat, capital-return committee, mutual non-disparagement.

options.label: Launch the proxy fight
pros: Winner takes the whole board agenda
Your thesis gets a shareholder verdict
cons: Burns enormous cash on solicitation
Losing the vote ends the campaign dead
options.consequence: You nominate a full slate; Meridian files its proxy calling your fund 'a self-dealing raider.'

beats.title: Swing holders and ISS
beats.situation: The vote math lives on the war room whiteboard: index funds 28%, ISS-followers 20%, retail 15%. Whoever wins the middle wins Meridian.
beats.debateTopic: Where do we spend the final persuasion budget?

scriptedLines.text: ISS moves twenty points of the vote in one report. Nothing else comes close.
The index funds won't meet twice. One pitch, perfect, or nothing.

options.label: Pitch ISS and Glass Lewis
pros: One recommendation swings 20% of the vote
Proxy advisors love a governance story
cons: All-or-nothing meeting
Their process is a black box
options.consequence: ISS recommends FOR two of your nominees, citing 'sustained underperformance and board entrenchment.'

options.label: Court the index funds directly
pros: 28% of the register in three meetings
Stewardship teams already dislike the pill era
cons: Institutionally cautious — they default to management
No public momentum even if they flip
options.consequence: Two of the big three stewardship teams take the second meeting. That never happens.

options.label: Run a retail media blitz
pros: 15% retail skews anti-incumbent
Cheap impressions via financial TV
cons: Retail rarely returns proxy cards
High heat invites regulator attention
options.consequence: Your fund's campaign site and TV hits trend; #FixMeridian does numbers.

beats.title: Endgame vote
beats.situation: Annual meeting day. The boardroom is standing-room only. The inspector of elections is ready. This is where the campaign ends — one way or the other.
beats.debateTopic: Force the vote, ratify the deal, or take the last-minute compromise?

scriptedLines.text: The meeting will come to order. We have one item of business that matters.
Whatever happens today, I built this company. Remember that.
Final tally projections are on your phone. It's going to be close.

options.label: Force the vote on your slate
pros: Total victory rewrites the whole board
Your mandate becomes undeniable
cons: Vote-day surprises are legendary
No fallback if the tally breaks wrong
options.consequence: Preliminary tally: your nominees carry the vote. Hale concedes at the podium.

options.label: Ratify the settlement on stage
pros: Certain, clean, and value-accretive
Board partnership for the breakup ahead
cons: Less upside than total board control
Critics call it a half-win
options.consequence: The settlement is ratified to applause; joint statement promises 'a new chapter at Meridian.'

options.label: Take the eleventh-hour compromise
pros: Salvages something from a weak hand
Keeps the relationship for round two
cons: Smallest value unlock of the three
Street writes the campaign off as a draw
options.consequence: A midnight compromise: one observer seat and a capital-return study. The tape shrugs.
